UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.          )       Docket No. ER26-3380-000




             PROTEST AND REQUEST FOR REJECTION OF FILING
            OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE FOR EVIDENTIARY HEARINGS
                   AND/OR SETTLEMENT PROCEEDINGS BY
                 OFFICE OF THE OHIO CONSUMERS’ COUNSEL




                                 Maureen Willis
                                 Ohio Consumers’ Counsel

                                 Angela O’Brien
                                 Deputy Consumers’ Counsel

                                 Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel
                                 65 East State Street, Suite 700
                                 Columbus, Ohio 43215
                                 Telephone: (614) 466-9531
                                 angela.obrien@occ.ohio.gov

                                 Denise C. Goulet
                                 McCarter & English, LLP
                                 1301 K Street, N.W.

                                 Special Counsel to the Ohio Office of the Attorney
                                 General for the Office of the Ohio Consumers’
                                 Counsel


August 21, 2026
                              UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                              )        Docket No. ER26-3380-000




                PROTEST AND REQUEST FOR REJECTION OF FILING
               OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE FOR EVIDENTIARY HEARINGS
                      AND/OR SETTLEMENT PROCEEDINGS BY
                    OFFICE OF THE OHIO CONSUMERS’ COUNSEL



        PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM’s”) application in this case to implement a one-

time Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) program to acquire new generating capacity

needed to serve forecasted Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) and other large data center loads should

not be adopted.1 It will unreasonably shift the risks and costs associated with acquiring that new

capacity from the data center loads to existing consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM. The

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) should reject the filing because it fails to

protect Ohio consumers and other consumers in PJM from the risks associated with this new

forecasted load, and from the associated costs of serving these loads. PJM’s proposal will result

in excessive, unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory and preferential rates for existing

consumers.

        In the alternative, FERC should set PJM’s filing for evidentiary hearings and/or

settlement proceedings so that PJM and stakeholders can adequately consider and vet alternative

proposals for acquiring needed new supply for AI and other large data center loads, including



1
 This Protest is submitted pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Rules of Practice
and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211.
 proposals prepared by the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (“IMM”) and other consumer

representatives. Unlike PJM’s proposal in this case, the IMM’s and other parties’ competing,

well-founded proposals would properly guard against such unreasonable costs shifts and

excessive rates for existing consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM.

           The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel is the statutory representative of millions of

Ohio residential utility consumers, per R.C. Chapter 4911. OCC actively advocates for Ohioans

in numerous state and federal regulatory proceedings, including proceedings before FERC. OCC

timely intervened in this case on August 14, 2026.2 Ohio residential consumers may be adversely

affected if FERC accepts PJM’s filing in this case. PJM’s proposal would require them to pay for

resource inadequacy risks and related costs that they did not cause, i.e., risks and costs associated

with obtaining adequate generating capacity to satisfy the loads of new AI and large data center

customers.

      I.       BACKGROUND

           PJM submitted in this docket on July 31, 2026, a proposal for implementing a one-time

procurement of new generating capacity that PJM represents is needed to address “resource

adequacy challenges” in the PJM region.3 PJM states these shortages are associated with

insufficient commitments of capacity in the Reliability Pricing Mechanism (“RPM”) auctions for

the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years.4 PJM further represents that the insufficiency of

resources in these RPM auctions is “primarily driven by the unprecedented addition in recent

Ohio Consumers’ Counsel, available on FERC’s e-library website as Accession Document No. 20260814-5066.
3
 Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads, PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, available on FERC’s e-library website as Accession
Document No. 20260731-5214 (“RBP Application”).
4
    RBP Application at 1.



                                                       2
 years of large loads, most notably AI and other data centers, in the PJM region.”5 PJM states

that the proposal is consistent with the following goals agreed to by the National Energy

Dominance Council (“NEDC”) and 13 governors of the PJM states:

                     procure new capacity resources through a backstop auction;

                     that auction should commence no later than September 2026;

                     the auction should provide 15-year price certainty for new capacity resources;

                     the program should “allocate the cost of any new capacity procured through the
                      backstop auction to Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) with new data centers
                      located in their regions that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be
                      curtailable;6 and

                     the program should allocate any remaining costs associated with the shortage to
                      LSEs based on their remaining net shortages.7

            PJM states that its region hosts the largest concentration of data center load in the world,

and that its forecasted load is expected to increase by 32 gigawats (“GW”) between 2024 and

2030, with 30 GW driven solely by the large load data centers. It also asserts that the shortfall in

capacity cleared to meet the resource adequacy needs of the region has grown for each of the

past three RPM auction Delivery Years, which includes the 2028/2029 Delivery Year auction,

run in July of this year.8

            PJM proposes to implement a one-time auction along the lines of its existing RPM

backstop auction process to secure the difference between the RPM auction results for the

    Governors’ Principle.” PJM states that the governors support includes the 13 states of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana,
    Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, and West
    Virginia, and the District of Columbia.

 2028/2029 Delivery Year and the amount needed to serve forecasted load for that year. The

auction would obtain commitments of new capacity from eligible resources for a fixed term of

up to 15 years, starting with the 2028/2029 Delivery Year and ending with the 2042/2043

Delivery Year.9 The commitment term for the resources acquired in the auction that are

scheduled to commence service after the 2028/2029 Delivery Year will be shortened by a

commensurate number of years, as no commitment will extend beyond the 2042/2043 Delivery

Year.10 In effect, PJM proposes to allow planned new generating resources to participate in the

auction even if their in-service date in beyond the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, so long as those

resources are in-service by June, 2032.11

            PJM proposes to limit the auction to new load coming on-line in 2028/2029 that does not

bring its own capacity resources sufficient to serve its needs.12 “In other words, the RBP is a

one-time mechanism that will only procure the capacity necessary to cover any remaining

shortfall from the 2028/2029 BRA after PJM has accounted for new capacity being brought by

new load or that otherwise qualify for a limited opt-out from the RBP.”13

            The proposed auction will use a RTO region-wide target, and PJM would enter into long-

term agreements with the suppliers to purchase that capacity.14 PJM proposes to pay each seller

its offer bid, less any revenues the seller is entitled to receive for commitment of the same

capacity in the regular RPM auctions.15 New loads can acquire their own capacity by entering

RPM auction.16 Sellers into the auction will be responsible for all actual Network Upgrade costs

incurred to interconnect their resources to the grid.17

            PJM is not proposing to match acquired supply to individual new large loads but rather

proposes to allocate costs to Electric Distributor Company (“EDC”) zones where the new large

loads are located, and then to LSEs within that zone that are short of supply commitments.18

PJM then relies on the states to allocate these costs to retail customers within those LSE areas.19

If a state does not report obligations for new load within LSE regions in their jurisdictions, then

the zonal RBP charges will be to all consumers within the relevant zone.20

            If generators bidding in new supply fail to bring their new resources on-line as promised

in the offer, PJM proposes to impose a penalty on those entities equal to 20% of the proposed bid

price.21 If the new resources cannot come on-line within three years of the auction in which they

cleared, PJM will cancel the contract with that supplier. 22 PJM proposes that the shortage

penalties will be allocated to load.23 If LSEs default on payments, then PJM proposes that other

LSEs in the same EDC zone as the defaulting LSE that are short in that same year will pay the

amounts due.24

      II.      PROTEST

           OCC protests PJM’s filing because it will not minimize costs for consumer, nor

accomplish its objectives of acquiring new generating capacity in the region in a manner that

allocates risks and costs for the new capacity to those causing the costs to be incurred, i.e., AI

and large data center loads. Instead, the proposal will result in shifting these risks and costs to

existing consumers who have not caused the need for new generating capacity and who are

unlikely to use the generating capacity provided by these new resources. The risks and costs

include the realistic uncertainty that either generating capacity or the forecasted AI or large data

center loads will not show up. Moreover, the proposal inappropriately and unreasonably relies

on state laws and regulations, that may not exist in many states, to ensure that these costs and

risks in fact are borne by the AI and large data center loads.

           Ohio has no statutes governing allocation of large load-related generation capacity costs

among retail customers. And while there is one case in which the Public Utilities Commission of

Ohio (“PUCO”) has directed allocation of some of these large load driven costs and risks to the

large load data center customers, there are no uniform regulations and tariffs that apply to all

utilities and LSEs in the state.25 Thus, PJM’s proposed RBP program leaves many Ohio

consumers at significant risk of bearing costs associated with these new large data center loads.

In contrast, the backstop procurement proposal prepared by the PJM IMM and proposals

discussed by other stakeholders in PJM would directly allocate the risks and costs of this new




25
  In the Matter of the Application of Ohio Power Company for New Tariffs Related to Data Centers and Mobile
Data Centers, Opinion and Order (Jul. 9, 2925), in PUCO Case No. 24-508-EL-ATA; see also In the Matter of the
Application of Ohio Power Company for New Tariffs Related to The Standard Service Offer Service for Data Center
Load, Finding and Order (Aug. 5, 2026) in PUCO Case No. 26-113-EL-ATA. While there are additional matters
pending or contemplated to implement specific data center load tariffs for American Transmission Systems, Inc.,
Dayton Power and Light Company and Duke Energy Ohio, to date the PUCO has not adopted orders establishing
programs for these utilities.


                                                      6
 generating capacity to the new AI and large data center loads, while fulfilling the resource

adequacy needs of the region.

            OCC recognizes that PJM has proposed a myriad of rules for the RBP auction intended to

mitigate market power and control prices that OCC has not described here. While OCC is not

addressing in this protest every serious flaw raised by the PJM RBP proposal, OCC notes that the

overall RBP design is unlikely to mitigate market power or achieve the intended objective of

ensuring resource adequacy in a manner consistent with cost allocation principles and in a

manner that will result in just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory and preferential rates for

consumers. OCC generally supports the protest submitted in this docket by the Maryland Office

of People’s Counsel and other consumer advocates on issues not addressed directly in this

Protest.

                  A. PJM’s RBP proposal will not ensure just, reasonable rates for consumers;
                     nor will it prevent unduly discriminatory or preferential rates for consumers.

            PJM’s RBP proposal will not constrain capacity prices resulting from the RBP auction,

and will not protect existing consumers from the excessive costs and risks associated with those

auctions. One example is PJM’s proposed pay-as-bid approach for settling the RBP auction.26

PJM argues that this proposal is reasonable because the auction will not be procuring a uniform

commodity and a single clearing price would “transfer inframarginal rents to every seller priced

below the most expensive accepted offer.”27 These are extraordinary claims in light of PJM’s

support for the existing RPM rules that use a single clearing price approach.

            FERC has long found the existing offer and clearing price rules for the existing RPM

auctions just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Those RPM auctions


26
     Id. at 65.
27
     Id. at 65-66.



                                                    7
 similarly procure non-uniform commodities (new and existing generating capacity, storage

resources, intermittent resources, demand resources, etc.) as proposed for the RBP auction. They

also pay the single clearing price to all resources clearing at or below the clearing bid, thus

allowing all inframarginal units to receive payments above their offer bids. PJM’s purported

explanation for different rules for the RBP auctions does not address why it now needs to use a

clearing approach that is diametrically opposite what it has supported for over 20 years in its

RPM auctions. Mere statements as to what the new proposal would accomplish without an

explanation for why the disparate treatment is needed or appropriate is not consistent with

judicial mandates for reasoned departures from existing rules.

            Additionally, PJM argues that its proposed “maximum willingness-to-pay cap” will

provide “a direct limit on procurement costs even in the absence of offer mitigation.” 28

PJM proposes to set the cap at the maximum price for the existing RPM auctions of

$555/MW/day, arguing that this mitigates market power for consumers because

“competitive dynamics are expected to encourage suppliers to submit competitive offers

that more closely reflect their willingness to provide service.” 29

            That too is an extraordinary claim given that PJM is proposing this one-time RBP

auction because there is a 6,800 MW scarcity of supply in the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.

The $555/MW-day (unforced capacity) offer cap is based on scarcity conditions and is

significantly higher than the clearing price in the 2028/2029 auction of $325/MW-day

price cap, which also reflects the scarcity conditions in that auction. 30 Exactly what is it


28
     Id. at 68.
29
     Id. at 68-69.
30
  Id. at 62 for current $555/MW-day offer cap; see also 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction Report at 3 (Jul. 14,
2026), available at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2028-2029/2028-
2029-bra-results-report.pdf.



                                                        8
 that will constrain supplier incentives to bid at the price cap instead of their marginal

costs in this auction? The answer is: nothing. Current scarcity market conditions in

PJM’s capacity markets simply do not provide the tempering influence needed to mitigate

market power, and as is anticipated in non-scarce markets. PJM has not demonstrated

that its RBP proposal is designed to sufficiently mitigate market power and produce

prices for consumers that are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or

preferential. Instead, this market design appears guaranteed to result in excessive electric

capacity prices for consumers in PJM that will be allocated the costs of this auction.

            One of the most glaring flaws in PJM’s proposal is that by allowing resources that will

not come on-line until after the 2028/2029 Delivery Year to participate, it will not ensure

resource adequacy for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year – the year that new generating capacity is

most needed. PJM proposes to accept offers from planned generating resource owners whose

planned generation have commercial operation dates beyond the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, so

long as the resources have an in-service date no later than 2032.31 PJM states that it is necessary

to accept such offers because it is unlikely there are sufficient planned resources with in-service

dates that line up with the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.32 PJM maintains that allowing resources

with in-service dates beyond that Delivery Year to participate in the auction will mitigate

scarcity in the auction by increasing the otherwise available supply.33 PJM proposes that any

capacity shortfalls in the interim will be addressed by curtailment policies being proposed in




31
     RBP Application at 51.
32
     Id. at 68.
33
     Id.



                                                    9
 newly filed PJM Docket No. 26-3515-000, i.e., the Interim Resource Adequacy Service

(“IRAS”) proposal.34

            OCC agrees there is merit in PJM’s concern that scarcity conditions will exist in the RBP

auction. It is for this reason that sufficient market power mitigation rules must be in place to

protect those paying the costs of this auction. As explained above, PJM’s proposal fails to

ensure such mitigation. The proposal’s reliance on planned new generation resources that will

not be in-service by the 2028/2029 Delivery Year for market power mitigation does not address

concerns that the RBP auction is likely to clear at the extremely high price cap due to shortage

conditions. Instead, it means that resources available in the 2028/2029 Delivery Year are still

likely to be well short of supply needed for resource adequacy if the forecasted AI and large data

center loads come on-line as forecasted in that timeframe.

            PJM uses the scarcity concern as its main reason for rushing a FERC decision on the RBP

proposal.35 However, for the reasons explained in this protest, that proposal is unlikely to result

in reasonable costs for consumers and unlikely to adequately protect existing consumers from

excessive, unjust and unreasonable rates. PJM’s admits that its proposal is unlikely to resolve

the scarcity conditions for the near future because at least some of the newly-acquired generating

resources will not be in service in time for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year. So, there is no reason

for FERC to rush to put PJM’s proposed RBP auction in place by September 2026 as PJM

requests. Instead, FERC should set PJM’s proposed auction design for evidentiary hearings

and/or settlement proceedings and provide stakeholders and consumers an opportunity to explore

options that would better ensure resource adequacy at just and reasonable rates. The IRAS



34
     Id. at 48.
35
     Id. at 3-9.



                                                   10
 curtailment proposal in Docket No. ER26-3515 could better address timing concerns resulting

from delaying implementation of a backstop procurement auction.

         OCC is also concerned that PJM’s RBP proposal does little to rectify or minimize the

excessive costs existing consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM are paying due to RPM

auctions that have already been run for prior years. The IMM has calculated that data center

demand increased capacity costs to other PJM customers by approximately $23.1 billion across

the 2025/2026, 2026/2027, 2027/2028 Base Residual Auctions.36 The $23.1 billion figure is not

a mere historical artifact of load growth. It reflects a structural outcome of a capacity market in

which extraordinary new demand (data centers) can raise clearing prices across a much larger

base of existing capacity (other customers including residential customers). The result is a

system-wide cost shift that extends far beyond the incremental load that triggered it. The IMM’s

June 30, 2026 RBP proposal, discussed in section C below, demonstrates that significant reforms

to PJM’s RBP proposal are needed to stop the historical subsidies already being provided by

existing consumers to AI and large data center loads.

         Accordingly, the task should be not only to prevent future cost shifts from new data

center load, but also to evaluate whether and how PJM’s market design can better account for the

magnitude of subsidies already imposed on existing consumers. Consumer protection requires

more than prospective reform. PJM and FERC must confront the substantial costs already borne

by consumers because data-center demand has been incorporated into prior capacity auctions.37



36
  Monitoring Analytics, Critical Issue Fast Path Proposed Reliability Backstop Auction Proposal (Jun. 30, 2026),
available at
https://www.monitoringanalytics.com/reports/Presentations/2026/IMM%20Backstop%20auction%20design%20pro
posal%20-%20V6%202026.06.19.pdf (“IMM RBP Proposal”).
37
  Similarly, there is concern with the effect that data centers have had on the energy prices in PJM. Energy prices
have significantly increased in large part due to the 24 x 7/365 data center energy use pushing the marginal clearing
unit higher up in the PJM dispatch stack. In 2023, energy costs across PJM averaged $30.23/MWh. During the first


                                                         11
 For transparency regarding the magnitude of the problem, PJM and the IMM should develop a

standardized accounting of capacity costs attributable to data center demand in each affected

BRA for the past three to five Delivery Years.

            PJM and FERC should evaluate whether a legacy data center cost allocation and

consumer credit mechanisms could, consistent with cost causation and other rate principles,

assign identified legacy costs on a forward-looking basis to the load responsible for driving these

costs and risks and provide corresponding credits to existing customers that are bearing these

costs. Such a mechanism should be grounded in demonstrable cost causation and rate principles.

It should avoid arbitrary assignment of historical costs to unrelated new loads. And, to the extent

possible, it should ensure that any recovery amounts are returned to affected non-data center

customers. Where feasible, PJM should consider transitional charges on identifiable responsible

loads to recover a portion of legacy costs. The objective is consumer restitution through

principled cost allocation.

                B. The RBP proposal will unjustly and unreasonably leave existing consumers
                   in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM bearing the risks and costs associated with
                   these new AI and large data center load.

            PJM’s RBP proposal does not accomplish the objective of protecting existing consumers

from the risks and costs associated with procuring new generating capacity for AI and large data

center loads. Instead, the proposal is designed to allocate the costs of the auction to all

consumers in the EDC’s zone where the AI and large data center loads that bring insufficient

generating capacity with them are located.38 Yet many of those consumers are no more




seven months of 2026, energy costs across PJM averaged $72.07/MWh. PJM and FERC should also confront these
costs and should evaluate whether a legacy cost allocation and customer credit mechanism should be adopted.
38
     Id. at 96-97.



                                                    12
 responsible for the incurrence of these costs than are consumers in regions where there is no

shortage of capacity for AI and large data center loads.

           PJM inappropriately relies on state programs to determine allocation among retail

consumers within these zones. In other words, PJM is asking FERC to punt the question of cost

allocation for these new resources to the states. However, as indicated earlier in this Protest, not

all states have statutes that would allocate these costs to the AI and large data centers driving the

cost incurrence. As note earlier, Ohio is one such state. The PUCO has required a special tariff

to allocate to AI and large data center loads the costs of new generating capacity and other

resources needed to serve them from only one of four utilities serving retail consumers in Ohio,

i.e.. American Electric Power.39 No similar protections exist currently for consumers of the three

other utilities in the state. There is no guarantee under Oho law that all Oho consumers will be

protected against the cross-subsidies inherent in PJM’s proposal. It is fundamentally

unreasonable for PJM to rely on a system of shared state-federal jurisdiction to resolve a

problem raised directly by its proposed wholesale RBP program.

           PJM’s proposed penalty structure for ensuring that generation suppliers submitting sell

offers into the RBP auction abide by their offer commitments is similarly unjust, unreasonable,

and unduly discriminatory and preferential. While it is reasonable for PJM to propose shortage

penalties for a supplier’s failure to come on-line by the anticipated commercial operation date

encompassed in its offer, it is not reasonable for PJM to impose those shortage charges and costs

on all loads in the EDC and LSE zones experiencing shortages.40 The purpose of shortage

penalties should be to strongly encourage generation capacity sellers to abide by their



39
     Supra, n.25.
40
     RBP Application at 61 (“Shortfall charges assessed to RBP Resources will be allocated to load”).



                                                          13
 commitments to supply power by a date certain. OCC understands that events can occur to delay

such commercial operation dates. But the risks of such events should be borne by those with

more direct control over such events, i.e., the suppliers themselves.

        Allowing those costs to be transferred to load essentially just shifts the risk that a

generating resource will be commercially operational to the parties with no control over those

operations, i.e., the loads that must bear the costs of the power to be generated. Moreover, that

shift in risk and costs shields the generators, the entities with at least some control over the

process of bringing this generation online, from the costs of their actions or inactions. In the

event of a supplier’s failure to reach a targeted commercial operation deadline, existing load is

already bearing a significant portion of that risk by having to forego the needed capacity and

likely being subjected to curtailment of use. To impose the shortage charges on those loads, in

addition to the shortage conditions, is fundamentally unjust, unreasonable and unduly

discriminatory and preferential. Such a policy allows the suppliers to escape any financial risk or

responsibility for their investments. This violates FERC’s long-held policy of imposing the risk

of investment on those making the investments and away from loads who have no control over

those investments.41

        Additionally, PJM’s proposal to limit the shortage penalty to 20% of the offer price for

the capacity is also unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory and preferential in favor of

suppliers. The objective of such penalties should be to protect the load that will suffer from the

capacity shortages in the region. Electric generation capacity is a fundamental financial and



41

at P 1 (2009) (Effective wholesale competition protects consumers by providing more supply options, encouraging
new entry and innovation, spurring deployment of new technologies, promoting demand response and energy
efficiency, improving operating performance, exerting downward pressure on costs, and shifting risk away from

markets.”).


                                                      14
 health necessity for residential, commercial and industrial consumers in today’s economy,

especially for hospitals, schools, nursing homes and residential homes that have family members

living on electric-operated life support facilities. PJM’s proposal to limit the proposed shortage

penalty to only 1/5th of the cost of the capacity sell offer seriously undervalues the reliance load

places on resource adequacy. FERC should reject PJM’s proposed penalties for failure of

suppliers to live up to their capacity commitments when bidding planned resources into the RBP

auctions as fundamentally insufficient to protect consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM.

              C. The IMM proposed approach to resource adequacy in PJM will ensure
                 direct allocation of the risk and costs of needed new generation to the
                 responsible AI and large data center loads in the region.

           On June 30, 2026, Monitoring Analytics, the PJM IMM, posted on its website its

proposal for resolving the resource inadequacy concerns created by the shortages in the

2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years. The IMM submitted this proposal to the PJM Critical

Issue Fast Path stakeholder process as an alternative to the PJM RBP proposal.42 As the IMM

states, “[t]he most important criterion for evaluating proposals to address how to reliably serve

new data center load is the assignment of the costs and risks associated with LSEs serving data

center load.”43 The IMM explains that “the failure to exclude new data center load from the

BRAs [RPM base residual auctions], as PJM proposes, would by definition impose significant

costs on other customers and therefore violate the basic principle that data center costs should

not be imposed on other customers.”44

           By including AI and large data center loads in the RBP and other RPM auctions, PJM is

placing all existing consumers in the region at risk of paying for the capacity shortages because


42
     IMM RBP Proposal at 1.
43
     Id.
44
     Id.



                                                 15
 the costs of RPM and the proposed RBP auctions are to be spread across all consumers in the

regions that are short regardless of the driving cost causers for those shortages. Those costs and

risks include not only the cost of the procured generation, but the risks that both the new

generating capacity and the forecasted AI and large data center loads will not materialize.

            In contrast, the IMM proposes that LSEs serving the new AI and large data center loads

enter into 15-year bilateral contracts in which the risks and costs of the new generation to be

acquired to serve those loads are allocated only to the parties to those contracts.45 The IMM

explains that this proposal is analogous to the program in which Fixed Resource Requirements

customers opt-out of the RPM auctions.46 In essence, this proposal establishes a Bring Your

Own New Generation approach to solve the dire resource inadequacy concerns raised by the

exponential growth in AI and large data center loads on the PJM system in recent years.47

            To the extent that the affected LSEs do not enter into such contracts, the IMM proposes a

RBP construct that would “run a full single clearing price auction using the RPM capacity

market clearing model for just data center load.”48 In other words, the IMM proposal would

create an auction limited to new generating capacity supplies and new AI and large data center

loads, thus shielding existing consumers from the associated costs and risks imposed by these

way by the auction clearing process.

     III.      CONCLUSION

            FERC may accept or reject a utility filing under section 205 of the Federal Power Act, 16

U.S.C. 824d, depending on whether the utility has demonstrated that its proposal is just,

reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.59 However, as PJM notes in its RBP

Application, FERC may not modify substantial elements of the proposal without PJM’s

consent.60

            Although OCC seeks rejection of PJM’s proposal in this case, OCC agrees that

something must be done soon to address the resource adequacy concerns in the PJM region over

the next few years. Consequently, OCC urges that if FERC accepts the filing, it should do so

subject to refund and set the filing for hearing and/or settlement proceedings with directives that

the parties use the IMM RBP proposal as a starting point.

            Such a process will provide stakeholders an opportunity, subject to Settlement Judge

oversight, to develop a just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential solution

that will protect existing consumers in Ohio and elsewhere from the unreasonable shift of AI and

large data center load risks and costs to them, and from excessive, unjust, unreasonable and

unduly discriminatory and preferential rates.
